content: Congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) was first identified in 1941 as a complication of rubella infection in pregnant women who contracted the virus early in their pregnancy. An Australian ophthalmologist established the link and documented 78 cases of congenital cataracts in infants born to mothers infected with rubella during early pregnancy. The pathogenesis of CRS is multifactorial. Pregnant women who are not vaccinated against rubella are at high risk of contracting the infection. If infected during pregnancy, the rubella virus can cross the placenta and infect the fetus, disrupting normal organogenesis. The severity of fetal malformations depends on the gestational age at the time of infection. The highest risk of fetal anomalies, spontaneous abortion, or stillbirth occurs if the infection happens before conception or within the first 8–10 weeks of gestation. Rubella virus, the causative agent of CRS, is a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus (ssRNA) and the sole member of the genus Rubivirus within the family Togaviridae. While rubella has been largely eradicated in many developed countries due to widespread vaccination, it remains a significant health issue in developing regions where the MMR vaccine is not readily available. CRS affects multiple organ systems, with the classic triad of symptoms being cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss, and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Other findings include low birth weight, skin lesions, hepatosplenomegaly, and craniofacial abnormalities such as microcephaly or hydrocephalus. Differentiating CRS from other congenital infections, particularly the TORCH group (toxoplasmosis, other infections, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus), is essential due to overlapping clinical features. The incidence of CRS is difficult to estimate, especially in regions where rubella has been eliminated. In countries without rubella immunization programs, the incidence is estimated to range from 60 to 220 cases per 100,000 live births. There is no specific screening test for CRS. Prenatal testing may involve direct isolation of the virus, detection of viral nucleic acids, or identification of rubella-specific antibodies in fetal blood through invasive techniques such as amniocentesis, fetal blood sampling, or chorionic villus sampling. Postnatal testing includes isolating the virus from throat or urine cultures and detecting rubella-specific IgG or IgM antibodies. Additional laboratory findings in affected infants may include thrombocytopenia and elevated levels of PT, PTT, and bilirubin. Imaging studies can provide further insights. Chest X-rays may reveal increased pulmonary vascularity and cardiomegaly due to ventricular enlargement, depending on the size and type of associated heart defect. CT scans and MRIs are useful for assessing craniofacial abnormalities, such as microcephaly or hydrocephalus, and evaluating the brain. Multi-detector CT scans (MDCT) can detect cardiac anomalies like PDA and other associated defects. Echocardiography can identify cardiac abnormalities, including PDA, pulmonary artery stenosis, coarctation of the aorta, and septal defects (VSD or ASD). Prenatal ultrasound, while not highly sensitive, is specific for detecting anomalies such as intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), fetal hydrops, microcephaly, and cardiac or ophthalmic defects. There is no specific medical treatment for CRS. Surgical interventions may be required to address complications such as cardiac defects, cataracts, or hearing loss. Primary prevention through MMR vaccination prior to pregnancy is the most effective strategy to prevent CRS. Secondary prevention involves isolating infants with CRS during their hospital stay and ensuring that all healthcare workers and caregivers are immune to rubella.
